tool.name: JavaScript
tool.tagline: The language of the web, running in every browser and on servers via Node.js
tool.description: JavaScript (standardised as ECMAScript) is a dynamic, multi-paradigm language that runs in every web browser and, through runtimes like Node.js, Deno and Bun, on servers and tooling too. It powers interactive pages, web apps, APIs and build tools, and it is the foundation for TypeScript, React and most of the modern web stack.

concepts.name: Running JavaScript
concepts.summary: Run your first JavaScript in the browser console, in a web page and with Node.js.
concepts.why: Before anything else you need a fast loop of writing a line, running it and seeing the result.
concepts.body:
JavaScript runs wherever there is a **JavaScript engine**: V8 in Chrome, Edge and Node.js, SpiderMonkey in Firefox, JavaScriptCore in Safari and Bun. The language itself is standardised as **ECMAScript**; browsers add web APIs such as the DOM, and server runtimes add file and network APIs.

The quickest place to experiment is the browser's DevTools console (F12, then the Console tab): type an expression, press Enter, see its value. For a real page, put the code in its own file and load it with a script tag:

```html
<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>
```

`type="module"` makes the file an ES module: it is deferred until the HTML has been parsed, runs in strict mode and can use `import`. For a classic script, add `defer` so it does not block parsing.

On the command line, install Node.js and run `node app.js`, or just `node` for an interactive prompt (a REPL).

A program is a sequence of **statements**. Semicolons end statements; the engine inserts missing ones (automatic semicolon insertion), but most teams either always write them or use a formatter such as Prettier to keep things consistent. Comments are `// to end of line` or `/* block */`.

`console.log()` is your print statement in every environment, and `console.table()` and `console.error()` are handy variations.
takeaways: Use the DevTools console or the Node REPL to try ideas instantly
Load page scripts with `type="module"` (or `defer`) so they don't block HTML parsing
`console.log` works in every JavaScript environment
pitfalls: Putting a plain `<script src>` in the `<head>` without `defer`: it blocks parsing and runs before the elements it needs exist.

quiz.q: You load app.js with a plain <script src="app.js"> in the <head>, and it can't find elements in the body. Which change fixes it most simply?
options: Wrap the code in a try/catch
quiz.explain: defer (and module scripts) run after the document has been parsed, so the body elements exist.

concepts.name: Values and types
concepts.summary: The seven primitive types, objects, typeof, and which values count as truthy or falsy.
concepts.why: Every bug about unexpected comparisons or 'undefined is not a function' starts with not knowing what type a value has.
concepts.body:
JavaScript is **dynamically typed**: variables don't have types, values do. Every value is either an **object** or one of seven **primitives**:

- `string` — text, `"hi"`
- `number` — 64-bit floating point, `42`, `3.14`, `NaN`
- `bigint` — arbitrary-size integers, `10n`
- `boolean` — `true` / `false`
- `undefined` — "no value assigned"
- `null` — "intentionally empty"
- `symbol` — unique identifiers

Everything else — arrays, functions, dates, plain `{}` — is an object.

Primitives are immutable and compared by value: `"a" === "a"` is true. Objects are compared by **reference**: two separate `{}` are never equal, even with identical contents.

`typeof` tells you the type as a string. It has two famous quirks: `typeof null` is `"object"` (a bug kept for compatibility) and `typeof` of a function is `"function"`. Use `Array.isArray(x)` for arrays and `x === null` for null.

When a value is used as a condition, it is converted to a boolean. Exactly these values are **falsy**: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `"0"`, `"false"`, `[]` and `{}`.

Calling a method on a primitive, as in `"abc".toUpperCase()`, works because the engine temporarily wraps it in an object (`String`). You never need `new String()` yourself.
concepts.code:
console.log(typeof "hi");        // "string"
console.log(typeof 42);          // "number"
console.log(typeof 42n);         // "bigint"
console.log(typeof undefined);   // "undefined"
console.log(typeof null);        // "object"  (historic quirk)
console.log(typeof [1, 2]);      // "object"
console.log(typeof (() => {}));  // "function"
console.log(Array.isArray([1])); // true

console.log({} === {});          // false: different objects
console.log(Boolean(""), Boolean("0"), Boolean([])); // false true true
takeaways: Seven primitives plus objects; primitives compare by value, objects by reference
Falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN — everything else is truthy
`typeof null === "object"`; test arrays with `Array.isArray`
pitfalls: Assuming an empty array or object is falsy — `if ([])` runs its body.

quiz.q: What does typeof null return?
quiz.explain: It is a long-standing quirk of the language: typeof null is "object", so check null with === null.

quiz.q: Which of these values is truthy?
quiz.explain: Only the empty string is a falsy string; "0" is a non-empty string and therefore truthy.

concepts.name: Variables: let and const
concepts.summary: Declare variables with const and let, know what var does differently, and what const really protects.
concepts.why: Declarations decide where a name is visible and whether it can change, which shapes every line you write.
concepts.body:
Modern JavaScript declares variables with two keywords:

- `const` — the binding cannot be reassigned. Use it by default.
- `let` — the binding can be reassigned. Use it when the value really changes, like a loop counter or an accumulator.

Both are **block-scoped**: a variable declared inside `{ ... }` (an `if`, a loop, a bare block) does not exist outside it.

`const` makes the *name* constant, not the value. If a `const` holds an object or array, you can still change its contents — `const list = []; list.push(1)` is fine. Only `list = []` is an error.

Accessing a `let` or `const` before its declaration line throws a `ReferenceError`; the region before the declaration is called the **temporal dead zone**. This catches ordering bugs early.

You will also meet `var` in older code. It is **function-scoped** rather than block-scoped, can be re-declared, and is readable (as `undefined`) before its declaration. Those properties cause subtle bugs, so don't use `var` in new code.

Names are case-sensitive, conventionally `camelCase` (`userName`), and may contain letters, digits, `$` and `_`, but cannot start with a digit. `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` is common for true module-level constants like `MAX_RETRIES`.

A variable declared but not assigned holds `undefined`. Declaring several at once (`let a = 1, b = 2;`) works, but one per line is easier to read.
takeaways: Default to `const`; use `let` only when you reassign
`let`/`const` are block-scoped; `var` is function-scoped — avoid it
`const` prevents reassignment, not mutation of the object it points to
pitfalls: Thinking `const arr = []` makes the array read-only — it only fixes the binding.

quiz.q: const items = [1]; items.push(2); — what happens?
quiz.explain: const only prevents reassigning the name; the array it refers to can still be mutated.

concepts.name: Operators and equality
concepts.summary: Arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, and why you use === instead of ==.
concepts.why: Equality and coercion rules are the most common source of surprising results in JavaScript.
concepts.body:
The arithmetic operators are `+ - * /`, plus `%` (remainder) and `**` (power). Each has a compound assignment form: `x += 2`, `x **= 2`, and `++`/`--` add or subtract one.

`+` is special: if either operand is a string, it **concatenates**. So `"5" + 3` is `"53"`, while `"5" - 3` is `2` because `-` only does math and converts the string to a number.

Comparison uses `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` and two kinds of equality:

- `===` and `!==` (**strict equality**): true only if both type and value match. No conversion.
- `==` and `!=` (loose equality): convert operands first using rules that produce results like `0 == ""` being true.

Always use `===`. The one idiom some teams allow is `x == null`, which is true for both `null` and `undefined`.

`NaN` is not equal to anything, including itself; test it with `Number.isNaN(x)`. `Object.is(a, b)` is like `===` but treats `NaN` as equal to itself and distinguishes `0` from `-0`.

The logical operators `&&`, `||` and `!` short-circuit and return one of their **operands**, not necessarily a boolean:

- `a || b` returns `a` if it is truthy, otherwise `b`.
- `a && b` returns `a` if it is falsy, otherwise `b`.

That's why `name || "Anonymous"` works as a default. `!!x` converts any value to a boolean.
concepts.code:
console.log(7 % 3, 2 ** 10);    // 1 1024
console.log("5" + 3);           // "53"  (string concatenation)
console.log("5" - 3);           // 2     (numeric)

console.log(0 == "");           // true  (loose: avoid)
console.log(0 === "");          // false (strict)
console.log(null == undefined); // true
console.log(NaN === NaN);       // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN)); // true

const input = "";
console.log(input || "default"); // "default"
console.log("a" && "b");          // "b"
console.log(!!"text");            // true
takeaways: Use `===`/`!==`; loose `==` converts types in surprising ways
`+` concatenates if either side is a string; other math operators convert to numbers
`||` and `&&` return one of their operands, which makes them handy for defaults
pitfalls: Comparing with `=== NaN`, which is always false — use `Number.isNaN`.

quiz.q: What does "5" + 3 evaluate to?
quiz.explain: When either operand of + is a string, the other is converted to a string and they are concatenated.

quiz.q: What does 0 || "fallback" return?
quiz.explain: || returns the first truthy operand; 0 is falsy, so the right-hand side is returned.

concepts.name: Strings and template literals
concepts.summary: Create strings, interpolate with template literals and use the everyday string methods.
concepts.why: Most programs spend a lot of time building, slicing and checking text.
concepts.body:
Strings can use single quotes, double quotes or backticks. Backticks create **template literals**, which allow interpolation with `${expression}` and can span multiple lines:

```javascript
const msg = `Hello ${user.name}, you have ${count + 1} items`;
```

Strings are **immutable**: every method returns a new string and leaves the original alone. The ones you'll use constantly:

- `length`, `str[0]`, `str.at(-1)` (negative indexes count from the end)
- `includes`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `indexOf`
- `slice(start, end)` — end is exclusive; negatives count from the end
- `toUpperCase`, `toLowerCase`, `trim`, `trimStart`, `trimEnd`
- `split(separator)` to get an array, and `array.join(sep)` to go back
- `replace` (first match) and `replaceAll` (every match)
- `padStart(len, ch)` for things like zero-padding: `"7".padStart(3, "0")` is `"007"`
- `repeat(n)`

Comparison with `<` and `>` compares UTF-16 code units, so `"Z" < "a"` is true. For human-facing sorting use `a.localeCompare(b)` or `Intl.Collator`.

One Unicode gotcha: `length` counts UTF-16 code units, so an emoji outside the basic plane (like `"😀"`) has length 2. Iterating with `for...of` or spreading `[...str]` walks whole code points instead, which is what you usually want for user text.

Escape sequences such as `\n` (newline) and `\t` (tab) work in all three quote styles.
concepts.code:
const name = "Ada Lovelace";
console.log(`Hi ${name.split(" ")[0]}!`); // Hi Ada!

console.log(name.length);            // 12
console.log(name.slice(0, 3));       // "Ada"
console.log(name.at(-1));            // "e"
console.log(name.includes("Love"));  // true
console.log(name.toUpperCase());     // "ADA LOVELACE"

const csv = " a, b ,c ";
console.log(csv.split(",").map(s => s.trim())); // [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
console.log("2-5-2025".replaceAll("-", "/"));   // "2/5/2025"
console.log(String(7).padStart(3, "0"));        // "007"

console.log("😀".length, [..."😀"].length);      // 2 1
takeaways: Template literals: backticks plus `${expr}` for interpolation and multi-line text
String methods never modify the original — they return a new string
`length` counts UTF-16 units; use `[...str]` to count characters users see as one
pitfalls: Calling `str.replace("a", "b")` and expecting every match replaced — use `replaceAll`.

quiz.q: const s = "hello"; s.toUpperCase(); console.log(s); — what is logged?
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable; toUpperCase returns a new string that this code throws away.

concepts.name: Numbers, Math and BigInt
concepts.summary: How JavaScript numbers work, parsing and formatting them, and when you need BigInt.
concepts.why: Money, IDs and user input all hit the edges of floating point sooner or later.
concepts.body:
Every `number` is a 64-bit IEEE-754 double. There is no separate integer type, so `1` and `1.0` are the same value. Integers are exact up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1); beyond that, adjacent integers can't all be represented.

Decimal fractions are approximations: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. For money, compute in integer cents (or use a decimal library) and only format at the end.

Special values: `Infinity`, `-Infinity` and `NaN` ("not a number"), which results from invalid math like `0 / 0` or `Number("abc")`.

Converting text to numbers:

- `Number("42")` converts the whole string and returns `NaN` if anything is left over.
- `parseInt("42px", 10)` and `parseFloat` read a leading number and ignore the rest. Always pass the radix to `parseInt`.

Useful helpers: `Number.isInteger`, `Number.isFinite`, `Math.round/floor/ceil/trunc`, `Math.max/min`, `Math.random()` (0 inclusive to 1 exclusive). `n.toFixed(2)` rounds for display and returns a **string**.

For display to humans use `Intl.NumberFormat`, which handles separators, currencies and locales: `new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(1234.5)` gives `"$1,234.50"`.

When you need exact integers larger than 2^53 — database IDs, cryptography — use **BigInt**: write `123n` or `BigInt("123")`. BigInts can't be mixed with numbers in arithmetic (`1n + 1` throws), so convert explicitly. Numeric separators (`1_000_000`) work for both.
concepts.code:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);                  // 0.30000000000000004
console.log((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2));     // "0.30" (a string)

console.log(Number("12px"));             // NaN
console.log(parseInt("12px", 10));       // 12
console.log(Number.isNaN(0 / 0));        // true

const priceCents = 1999 * 3;             // compute money in integers
const fmt = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" });
console.log(fmt.format(priceCents / 100)); // "$59.97"

console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2); // 9007199254740992 (wrong!)
console.log(9007199254740991n + 2n);      // 9007199254740993n
const big = 1_000_000n * BigInt(3);       // convert before mixing
console.log(big);                         // 3000000n
takeaways: All numbers are doubles: fractions are approximate, integers are safe up to 2^53 − 1
`Number()` is strict, `parseInt(str, 10)` reads a numeric prefix
Format for people with `Intl.NumberFormat`; use BigInt for huge exact integers
pitfalls: Treating the result of `toFixed` as a number — it is a string.

quiz.q: What do Number("12px") and parseInt("12px", 10) return?
quiz.explain: Number requires the whole string to be numeric, while parseInt reads the leading digits and stops.

concepts.name: Conditionals
concepts.summary: Branch with if/else, the ternary operator and switch.
concepts.why: Every program makes decisions; writing them clearly keeps logic readable.
takeaways: `if` converts its condition with truthy/falsy rules — be explicit when 0 or "" are valid
`cond ? a : b` is an expression; keep ternaries short
`switch` uses `===` and falls through without `break`
pitfalls: Forgetting `break` in a `switch`, so the next case runs too.

quiz.q: const x = "1"; switch (x) { case 1: console.log("one"); break; default: console.log("other"); } — what is logged?
quiz.explain: switch compares with strict equality, and the string "1" is not === the number 1.

concepts.name: Loops
concepts.summary: Repeat work with for, while, for...of and for...in, and control it with break and continue.
concepts.why: Iterating over collections is one of the most common things code does.
concepts.body:
The classic `for` loop has an initialiser, a condition and an update:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) console.log(i);
```

`while (cond) { ... }` repeats as long as the condition is truthy; `do { ... } while (cond)` always runs at least once.

For walking through collections, prefer **`for...of`**. It iterates over the *values* of any iterable — arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, NodeLists:

```javascript
for (const fruit of ["apple", "pear"]) console.log(fruit);
```

When you also need the index, use `for (const [i, fruit] of fruits.entries())`.

**`for...in`** is different: it iterates over the enumerable *property names* (keys, always strings) of an object, including inherited ones. Use it rarely, and never for arrays; for objects, `Object.keys(obj)` or `Object.entries(obj)` with `for...of` is clearer.

Two keywords control a loop from inside:

- `break` exits the loop immediately.
- `continue` skips to the next iteration.

Labels (`outer: for (...)` then `break outer`) let you break out of nested loops, but extracting a function and returning is usually clearer.

Declaring the loop variable with `let` or `const` gives each iteration its own binding — this matters when callbacks created in the loop run later. With `var`, they would all share one variable.

Arrays also have methods like `forEach`, `map` and `filter` that replace many loops; you'll meet them in the array-methods lesson.
takeaways: `for...of` iterates values of arrays, strings, Maps and other iterables
`for...in` iterates property names (strings) — avoid it for arrays
`break` exits, `continue` skips to the next iteration
pitfalls: Using `for...in` on an array and getting string indexes (and inherited keys) instead of the elements.

quiz.q: for (const x in ["a", "b"]) console.log(x); — what is printed?
options: Nothing; for...in doesn't work on arrays
quiz.explain: for...in yields property names, which are strings; use for...of to get the values.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: Declare functions, pass parameters with defaults, return values and treat functions as values.
concepts.why: Functions are the main unit of reuse and abstraction in JavaScript.
concepts.body:
A **function declaration** names a reusable block of code:

```javascript
function area(width, height = width) {
  return width * height;
}
```

Parameters are local variables. JavaScript doesn't check argument counts: missing arguments are `undefined`, extra ones are ignored. **Default parameters** (`height = width`) kick in when the argument is missing or explicitly `undefined` — not when it's `null`. A function without a `return` statement (or with a bare `return;`) returns `undefined`.

To accept any number of arguments, use a **rest parameter**: `function sum(...nums)` gives you a real array.

Functions are **first-class values**: you can store them in variables, put them in objects, pass them to other functions and return them from functions. A **function expression** creates one inline:

```javascript
const square = function (n) { return n * n; };
```

Passing a function to another function — a **callback** — is everywhere in JavaScript: `button.addEventListener("click", handleClick)`, `items.map(format)`. Note the missing parentheses: `handleClick` passes the function; `handleClick()` would call it immediately and pass its result.

Function declarations are **hoisted**: you can call them before the line where they are written. Function expressions assigned to `const` are not usable before that line.

Good functions are small, do one thing, and are named with a verb that says what they do: `formatPrice`, `isValidEmail`, `loadUser`. Prefer returning values over modifying outer variables; it makes functions easier to test and reuse.
takeaways: Missing arguments are `undefined`; defaults apply only to `undefined`
No `return` means the function returns `undefined`
Functions are values: pass `fn`, not `fn()`, when giving a callback
pitfalls: Writing `addEventListener("click", handle())`, which calls `handle` right away and registers its return value.

quiz.q: function f(a, b = 2) { return a + b; } — what is f(1, null)?
quiz.explain: Defaults only apply to undefined; null is passed through and 1 + null is 1 because null converts to 0.

quiz.q: A function body has no return statement. What does calling it evaluate to?
options: The value of its last expression
quiz.explain: Unlike some languages, JavaScript does not return the last expression; the result is undefined.

concepts.name: Arrow functions
concepts.summary: Write compact functions with =>, use implicit returns and know how arrows differ from regular functions.
concepts.why: Arrows are the default way to write callbacks in modern code.
concepts.body:
An **arrow function** is a shorter function expression:

```javascript
const double = (n) => n * 2;
```

The rules for the short forms:

- One parameter: parentheses are optional (`n => n * 2`); zero or several need them (`() => 42`, `(a, b) => a + b`).
- If the body is a single expression without braces, its value is **returned implicitly**.
- With braces, it's a normal block and you need an explicit `return`.
- To implicitly return an object literal, wrap it in parentheses: `() => ({ id: 1 })`. Without them, the braces are read as a block and `id: 1` as a label, so the function returns `undefined`.

Arrows shine as callbacks: `prices.map(p => p * 1.2)`, `setTimeout(() => save(), 500)`.

They are not just syntax sugar, though. Arrow functions:

- have no own `this` — they use the `this` of the surrounding code, which is exactly what you want in callbacks inside methods;
- have no own `arguments` object (use rest parameters);
- cannot be called with `new` and have no `prototype`.

Because of the `this` behaviour, don't use an arrow as an object method that needs to refer to its object; use method syntax (`{ total() { return this.a + this.b; } }`) instead. You'll see the full `this` rules in a later lesson.

A common style is: function declarations for named, top-level functions, and arrows for short inline callbacks.
takeaways: `x => expr` returns `expr` implicitly; a braced body needs `return`
Wrap object literals in parentheses: `() => ({ ... })`
Arrows have no own `this`, `arguments` or `prototype` and can't be used with `new`
pitfalls: Using an arrow function as an object method and finding `this` isn't the object.

quiz.q: What does (() => { value: 1 })() return?
quiz.explain: The braces are parsed as a function body containing a labelled statement, so nothing is returned.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.summary: Create arrays, read and update elements, and add, remove and find items.
concepts.why: Arrays are the everyday ordered collection for lists of anything.
concepts.body:
An **array** is an ordered list of values of any types: `const items = ["a", 2, { id: 3 }]`. Indexes start at 0; `items.length` is the count, and `items.at(-1)` gets the last element.

Arrays are mutable objects. The core methods for adding and removing:

- `push(x)` / `pop()` — add/remove at the end (fast).
- `unshift(x)` / `shift()` — add/remove at the start (shifts every element).
- `splice(start, deleteCount, ...newItems)` — remove and/or insert in the middle; **mutates** and returns removed items.
- `slice(start, end)` — returns a **copy** of a portion, without mutating.

Searching: `includes(x)` returns a boolean, `indexOf(x)` returns the index or `-1`. Both compare by value for primitives but by **reference** for objects, so `[{ id: 1 }].includes({ id: 1 })` is false. You'll use `find` with a callback for that in the array-methods lesson.

`concat` and `join(sep)` combine arrays and turn them into strings; `Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i)` builds `[0, 1, 2]`.

Because arrays are objects, assigning one to another variable copies the **reference**, not the elements: changing `b` after `const b = a` changes `a` too. Make a shallow copy with `[...a]` or `a.slice()`.

`typeof []` is `"object"`; use `Array.isArray()` to check. Assigning beyond the end (`arr[10] = x` on a short array) creates empty "holes" — avoid it. Arrays can be nested to make grids: `grid[row][col]`.
takeaways: Indexes start at 0; `at(-1)` reads from the end
`slice` copies, `splice` mutates — easy to mix up
Assigning an array copies the reference; copy with `[...arr]`
pitfalls: Expecting `includes` or `indexOf` to find an object by its contents — they compare references.

quiz.q: const a = [1, 2, 3]; const b = a; b.push(4); — what is a.length?
options: It throws because a is const
quiz.explain: a and b reference the same array, so pushing through b changes what a sees.

concepts.name: Objects
concepts.summary: Group related data in objects: create them, read and update properties, add methods and iterate.
concepts.why: Objects are JavaScript's fundamental data structure; nearly everything you work with is one.
concepts.body:
An **object** is a collection of key–value pairs called **properties**:

```javascript
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36, "favorite color": "green" };
```

Read and write properties with **dot notation** (`user.name`) or **bracket notation** (`user["favorite color"]`). Brackets are required when the key isn't a valid identifier or is stored in a variable: `user[field]`. Reading a missing property gives `undefined` rather than an error.

Object literals have handy shorthands:

- `{ name, age }` means `{ name: name, age: age }`.
- **Computed keys**: `{ [key]: value }`.
- **Methods**: `{ greet() { return "Hi " + this.name; } }`.

Add a property by assigning it, remove one with `delete obj.key`. Check whether a property exists with `Object.hasOwn(obj, "key")` (own properties only) or `"key" in obj` (includes inherited ones).

To iterate, convert to arrays: `Object.keys(obj)`, `Object.values(obj)`, `Object.entries(obj)`, usually with `for...of`. `Object.fromEntries(pairs)` goes the other way. Keys are strings (or symbols); numeric-looking keys are converted to strings and listed first in ascending order, then other strings in insertion order.

Like arrays, objects are handled by **reference**: passing an object to a function lets the function modify the caller's object. Copy shallowly with `{ ...obj }` or `Object.assign({}, obj)`.

Plain objects are ideal for records with known fields. For dictionaries with arbitrary keys that you add and remove frequently, a `Map` (covered later) is often a better fit.
takeaways: Dot notation for fixed names, brackets for dynamic or unusual keys
Shorthands: `{ name }`, `{ [key]: v }`, `{ method() {} }`
`Object.entries` + `for...of` is the idiomatic way to iterate an object
pitfalls: Writing `obj.key` when the key is in a variable — that looks up the literal property "key".

quiz.q: const field = "age"; const p = { age: 30 }; — which expression returns 30?
quiz.explain: Bracket notation evaluates the expression inside, so p[field] looks up the "age" property.

concepts.name: Optional chaining and ??
concepts.summary: Safely read through possibly-missing values with ?. and supply defaults with ?? and ??=.
concepts.why: Real data has gaps; these operators replace long chains of && checks and buggy || defaults.
concepts.body:
Reading a property of `undefined` or `null` throws a `TypeError`. **Optional chaining** `?.` stops evaluation and returns `undefined` if the value on its left is `null` or `undefined`:

```javascript
const city = user?.address?.city;   // undefined instead of a crash
```

It has three forms:

- `obj?.prop` — property access
- `obj?.[expr]` — bracket access
- `fn?.(args)` — call only if `fn` exists, e.g. `options.onDone?.()`

The **nullish coalescing** operator `a ?? b` returns `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`. Compare it with `||`, which falls back on *any* falsy value:

```javascript
const volume = settings.volume ?? 50; // keeps a valid 0
const bad = settings.volume || 50;    // 0 becomes 50!
```

Use `??` for defaults whenever `0`, `""` or `false` are legitimate values.

There are also **logical assignment** operators:

- `a ??= b` — assign only if `a` is null/undefined
- `a ||= b` — assign if `a` is falsy
- `a &&= b` — assign if `a` is truthy

They're handy for filling in defaults: `config.retries ??= 3`.

Don't sprinkle `?.` everywhere: if a value must exist, a crash with a clear error is more useful than an `undefined` that propagates silently. Use it where absence is genuinely expected — optional fields, API responses, optional callbacks.

One syntax note: you can't combine `??` with `||` or `&&` without parentheses; `a || b ?? c` is a SyntaxError.
takeaways: `?.` returns `undefined` instead of throwing when the left side is null or undefined
`??` defaults only for null/undefined; `||` also replaces 0, "" and false
`??=`, `||=`, `&&=` assign conditionally
pitfalls: Using `||` for a default when 0 or an empty string is a valid value.

quiz.q: const n = 0; — what are n ?? 5 and n || 5?
quiz.explain: ?? only replaces null and undefined, while || replaces any falsy value such as 0.

concepts.name: The DOM: finding and changing elements
concepts.summary: Select elements with querySelector, change their text, classes and attributes, and create new ones.
concepts.why: The DOM is how JavaScript reads and updates what the user sees on a web page.
concepts.body:
When a browser loads HTML it builds the **DOM** (Document Object Model): a tree of objects, one per element and text node, rooted at `document`. Changing those objects changes the page.

Find elements with CSS selectors:

- `document.querySelector(sel)` — the first match, or `null`.
- `document.querySelectorAll(sel)` — a static `NodeList` of all matches (it has `forEach` and works with `for...of`).
- Both also exist on elements, to search inside them: `form.querySelector("input")`.

Change what an element shows:

- `el.textContent = "..."` sets plain text. Safe with user input.
- `el.innerHTML = "..."` parses a string as HTML. **Never** use it with untrusted data — that is how cross-site scripting (XSS) happens.
- `el.classList.add/remove/toggle("active")` for styling via CSS classes; prefer this to setting `el.style` directly.
- `el.setAttribute("aria-expanded", "true")`, `el.hidden = true`, `input.value`, `img.src`.
- `el.dataset.userId` reads a `data-user-id` attribute.

Create and insert elements with `document.createElement("li")`, then `parent.append(child)` (also accepts strings), `prepend`, `before`, `after`, or `replaceWith`. Remove with `el.remove()`.

When you add many elements, build them first and append once (or use a `DocumentFragment`) so the browser updates layout once rather than many times.

Your script must run after the elements exist — use `type="module"` or `defer` on the script tag. If `querySelector` returns `null`, the element wasn't in the DOM yet or the selector is wrong.
takeaways: `querySelector`/`querySelectorAll` find elements with CSS selectors
Use `textContent` for text; `innerHTML` with user data is an XSS hole
Toggle `classList` instead of setting inline styles
pitfalls: Running the script before the HTML is parsed, so `querySelector` returns `null`.

quiz.q:
You want to show a user's comment inside a

. Which is the safe choice?
quiz.explain: textContent inserts the string as plain text, so any markup in it is never interpreted.

concepts.name: Handling events
concepts.summary: React to clicks, input and form submissions with addEventListener and the event object.
concepts.why: Interactivity in the browser is entirely driven by events.
concepts.body:
The browser fires **events** when things happen: clicks, key presses, input changes, form submissions, page load. You listen with `addEventListener`:

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => { ... });
```

The handler receives an **event object** describing what happened: `event.target` (the element where it originated), `event.key` for keyboard events, `event.clientX` for mouse position, and so on.

Some events have a **default action**: a link navigates, a form submits and reloads the page. Call `event.preventDefault()` to stop it, which is what you do when handling a form in JavaScript.

Common events to know:

- `click`, `dblclick`, `pointerdown`, `pointerup`
- `input` (fires on each change to a field) and `change` (when the edit is committed)
- `submit` on a form — listen here rather than on the button so Enter also works
- `keydown`, `keyup`
- `DOMContentLoaded` on `document`, `load` on `window`

To remove a listener, call `removeEventListener` with the **same function reference**, so keep the handler in a variable. The options object can help: `{ once: true }` removes it after the first call, and `{ signal }` with an `AbortController` removes it when you call `controller.abort()`.

Avoid inline `onclick="..."` attributes in HTML; they mix markup and behaviour and run in a confusing scope. Setting `el.onclick = fn` works but allows only one handler per event.

Read form values with `input.value` (always a string) or `new FormData(form)`, which collects every named field at once.
takeaways: `addEventListener(type, handler)` — the handler gets an event object
`event.preventDefault()` cancels default actions like form submission
Removing a listener needs the same function reference (or `{ once }` / `{ signal }`)
pitfalls: Listening to a submit button's `click` instead of the form's `submit`, so pressing Enter bypasses your code.

quiz.q: Why does this fail to remove the listener? btn.addEventListener("click", () => go()); btn.removeEventListener("click", () => go());
options: removeEventListener only works with { once: true }
Arrow functions can't be event listeners
Each arrow is a different function object, so it doesn't match the registered one
quiz.explain: Listeners are matched by function identity; two separately written arrows are different objects.

concepts.name: Array methods: map, filter, reduce
concepts.summary: Transform, filter, search, sort and group arrays with callback-based methods instead of hand-written loops.
concepts.why: These methods are the idiomatic way to process data in JavaScript and appear in nearly every codebase.
concepts.body:
Arrays have methods that take a **callback** and do the looping for you. The callback receives `(element, index, array)`.

Transforming and selecting — these return a **new array**:

- `map(fn)` — one output per input: `users.map(u => u.name)`.
- `filter(fn)` — keep elements where `fn` returns truthy.
- `flatMap(fn)` — map, then flatten one level; handy when each input yields 0..n outputs.

Searching:

- `find(fn)` / `findLast(fn)` — the first/last matching element, or `undefined`.
- `findIndex(fn)` — its index, or `-1`.
- `some(fn)` / `every(fn)` — booleans; they stop as soon as the answer is known.

Combining: `reduce((acc, x) => ..., initial)` folds the array into one value — a sum, an object, a lookup table. Always pass the initial value; without it, an empty array throws.

`forEach(fn)` just runs the callback; use it (or `for...of`) for side effects. It ignores return values and you can't `break` out of it.

Sorting has two traps. `sort()` **mutates** the array, and with no comparator it compares elements as strings, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass a comparator — `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers, `(a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)` for text — and use `toSorted()` (ES2023) when you want a sorted copy.

`Object.groupBy(items, fn)` (ES2024) groups elements into an object keyed by the callback's result.

Chain methods to build readable pipelines, but remember each step creates a new array; for huge datasets a single loop may be faster.
takeaways: `map`/`filter`/`flatMap` return new arrays; `find`/`some`/`every` search
`reduce` folds to one value — always pass an initial value
`sort` mutates and compares as strings by default; pass a comparator or use `toSorted`
pitfalls: Using `map` just to loop (ignoring the result) — use `forEach` or `for...of`.
Calling `sort()` on numbers without a comparator.

quiz.q: What does [10, 9, 1].sort() return?
quiz.explain: Without a comparator, elements are converted to strings and compared, and "10" sorts before "9".

quiz.q: Which method stops iterating at the first element that satisfies the callback and returns true?
quiz.explain: some short-circuits as soon as the callback returns a truthy value.

concepts.name: Destructuring, spread and rest
concepts.summary: Unpack arrays and objects into variables, and use ... to copy, merge and collect values.
concepts.why: Modern APIs, React props and function signatures are written with these patterns everywhere.
concepts.body:
**Destructuring** pulls values out of objects and arrays into variables, mirroring literal syntax:

```javascript
const { name, age } = user;          // by property name
const [first, second] = items;       // by position
```

Object patterns can rename (`{ name: userName }`), give **defaults** (`{ role = "guest" }`) and nest (`{ address: { city } }`). Array patterns can skip elements (`[, second]`) and swap variables: `[a, b] = [b, a]`. Defaults apply only when the value is `undefined`, not `null`.

Destructuring works in function parameters, which gives you named, optional arguments:

```javascript
function connect({ host = "localhost", port = 5432 } = {}) { ... }
```

The trailing `= {}` lets callers omit the argument entirely.

The `...` syntax means two opposite things depending on where it appears:

- **Rest** (in a pattern or parameter list) *collects* the remaining items: `const { password, ...safeUser } = user;` and `function log(level, ...messages)`.
- **Spread** (in a literal or call) *expands* an iterable or object: `[...a, ...b]`, `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }`, `Math.max(...nums)`.

With object spread, later properties win, which makes it the standard way to merge settings or produce an updated copy: `{ ...todo, done: true }`.

Spread copies are **shallow**: nested objects are still shared between the copy and the original. That matters when you update state immutably — copy each level you change.
takeaways: Destructure objects by name and arrays by position, with defaults and renames
`...` in a pattern collects (rest); in a literal or call it expands (spread)
Spread copies are shallow; later properties override earlier ones
pitfalls: Destructuring a parameter without `= {}` and then calling the function with no argument (TypeError).

quiz.q: const { a = 1 } = { a: null }; — what is a?
quiz.explain: Destructuring defaults only apply when the value is undefined; null is a real value and is kept.

quiz.q: After const copy = { ...orig }; copy.nested.x = 5; does orig.nested.x change?
options: No, spread makes a deep copy
Yes, because nested objects are shared by a shallow copy
It throws because orig is const
quiz.explain: Object spread copies top-level properties only, so copy.nested and orig.nested are the same object.

concepts.name: Scope and hoisting
concepts.summary: Understand lexical scope, block vs function scope, hoisting and the temporal dead zone.
concepts.why: Knowing where a name is visible explains a whole class of 'undefined' and ReferenceError bugs.
concepts.body:
JavaScript uses **lexical scope**: where a variable is visible is decided by where it is written in the source, not by how functions are called. Scopes nest, and a lookup walks outward from the innermost scope until it finds the name — or throws `ReferenceError`.

The kinds of scope:

- **Global** — names visible everywhere. `globalThis` is the global object in every environment.
- **Module** — each ES module has its own top-level scope; nothing leaks to the global unless you put it there.
- **Function** — parameters and everything declared inside.
- **Block** — `let`, `const` and `class` declarations inside `{ }`.

**Hoisting** describes the fact that declarations are processed when a scope is entered, before any code in it runs:

- Function declarations are hoisted completely; you can call them before their line.
- `var` declarations are hoisted and initialised to `undefined`, so reading one early silently gives `undefined`. `var` also ignores blocks and is scoped to the whole function.
- `let`, `const` and `class` are hoisted but *not initialised*. Touching them before the declaration throws a `ReferenceError`; that window is the **temporal dead zone** (TDZ).

An inner declaration with the same name **shadows** the outer one within its scope. That is legal but can be confusing; linters can flag it.

In non-module scripts, a top-level `var` or function declaration becomes a property of the global object, and assigning to an undeclared name creates a global in sloppy mode. Modules and strict mode turn the latter into an error — another reason to write modules.
takeaways: Scope is lexical: decided by where code is written
`var` is function-scoped and reads as `undefined` early; `let`/`const` throw in the TDZ
Function declarations are fully hoisted; function expressions are not
pitfalls: Relying on `var` inside an `if` or loop and expecting it to stay in that block.

quiz.q: Inside a function: console.log(x); let x = 1; — what happens?
quiz.explain: let bindings are in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs, so reading x throws.

concepts.name: Closures
concepts.summary: Functions remember the variables of the scope they were created in — use that for private state and factories.
concepts.why: Closures power callbacks, event handlers, module patterns, memoisation and React hooks.
takeaways: A closure is a function plus the variables in scope where it was defined
Closures capture variables, not snapshots of values
Use them for private state, factories and caches
pitfalls: Closing over a `var` loop variable in async callbacks — use `let`.

quiz.q: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); — what is printed?
quiz.explain: All three callbacks close over the same function-scoped var i, which is 3 when they run.

quiz.q: Why can't outside code change count in makeCounter's returned functions?
options: Closures copy count, so it is read-only
count only lives in makeCounter's scope, reachable solely via the closures
quiz.explain: The variable exists only in the enclosing function's scope; only functions created there can reach it.

concepts.name: How this works
concepts.summary: Learn the rules that decide what this refers to, and how call, apply, bind and arrows change it.
concepts.why: Losing this is one of the most frequent bugs in callbacks, event handlers and class methods.
concepts.body:
`this` is decided by **how a function is called**, not where it is defined (arrows are the exception). The rules, from most to least specific:

- **`new Fn()`** — `this` is the newly created object.
- **Explicit**: `fn.call(obj, a, b)`, `fn.apply(obj, [a, b])`, or a function made with `fn.bind(obj)` — `this` is `obj`.
- **Method call** `obj.method()` — `this` is `obj`, the thing before the dot.
- **Plain call** `fn()` — `this` is `undefined` in strict mode (modules and classes are always strict); in sloppy scripts it's the global object.

**Arrow functions** have no `this` of their own; they use the `this` of the enclosing scope at the time they are created.

The classic bug is **detaching a method**: `const f = obj.method; f()` is a plain call, so `this` is `undefined`. The same happens when you pass a method as a callback — `setTimeout(obj.method, 100)` or `button.addEventListener("click", counter.increment)`. Fixes:

- wrap it: `() => obj.method()`
- bind it: `obj.method.bind(obj)`
- in classes, define the handler as an arrow-function field: `increment = () => { ... }`

Inside a method, callbacks written as arrows see the method's `this`, which is why `this.items.forEach(item => this.render(item))` just works. A regular `function` callback there would get `undefined` instead.

In DOM listeners registered with a regular function, `this` is the element the listener is attached to (`event.currentTarget`). Reaching for `event.currentTarget` is clearer anyway.
takeaways: `this` comes from the call: `new`, explicit binding, `obj.method()`, or nothing
Arrow functions use the surrounding `this`
Passing `obj.method` as a callback loses `this` — wrap or bind it
pitfalls: Passing `this.handleClick` to `addEventListener` in a class without binding it.

quiz.q: In a module: const obj = { n: 1, get() { return this.n; } }; const g = obj.get; g(); — what happens?
quiz.explain: g() is a plain call, so this is undefined in strict code and reading undefined.n throws.

concepts.name: Classes
concepts.summary: Define classes with constructors, methods, fields, private members, static members and inheritance.
concepts.why: Classes are the standard way to model stateful objects and are used throughout the DOM and Node APIs.
concepts.body:
A **class** bundles a constructor and methods for creating objects of the same shape:

```javascript
class Account {
  #balance = 0;                 // private field
  static count = 0;             // shared by the class
  constructor(owner) { this.owner = owner; Account.count++; }
  deposit(amount) { this.#balance += amount; return this; }
  get balance() { return this.#balance; }
}
```

The pieces:

- `constructor` runs on `new Account("Ada")` and initialises the instance.
- **Methods** are shared by all instances.
- **Fields** (`name = value;`) are created per instance before the constructor body runs.
- **Private** members start with `#` and are inaccessible outside the class body — truly private, not a naming convention. `#field in obj` checks whether an object has one.
- **Getters/setters** (`get balance()`) look like properties to callers.
- **`static`** members belong to the class itself: `Account.count`, factory methods like `Account.fromJSON()`. A `static { }` block runs once for class setup.

**Inheritance** uses `extends`. A subclass constructor must call `super(...)` before it touches `this`; methods can call `super.method()` to extend the parent's behaviour. `instanceof` checks the chain: `savings instanceof Account`.

Classes are mostly syntax over prototypes (covered later), with differences: class bodies are always strict, classes can't be called without `new`, and class declarations are in the TDZ until defined (not hoisted like functions).

Prefer composition over deep hierarchies: one level of `extends` is common, three is a smell. And not everything needs a class — plain objects and functions are often simpler.
takeaways: Fields and `#private` members are declared in the class body
`extends` + `super()` for inheritance; call `super` before using `this`
`static` members live on the class; getters make computed properties
pitfalls: Forgetting `super()` in a subclass constructor (ReferenceError when `this` is used).

quiz.q: In a subclass constructor, what happens if you assign this.x = 1 before calling super()?
options: It works; super can be called later
quiz.explain: In a derived class, this is uninitialised until super() returns, so accessing it throws.

quiz.q: What is true of a field declared as #token in a class?
options: Code outside the class body cannot read it at all
It is shared by all instances
It is only private by convention
quiz.explain: # fields are enforced by the language; even obj["#token"] refers to an unrelated normal property.

concepts.name: Error handling
concepts.summary: Throw and catch errors, clean up with finally, create custom error types and add causes.
concepts.why: Robust programs fail loudly and recover deliberately instead of crashing or hiding problems.
takeaways: Throw `Error` objects (or subclasses), never strings
`finally` always runs — use it for cleanup
Wrap low-level errors with `{ cause }` instead of discarding them
pitfalls: An empty `catch {}` that hides bugs.
Expecting a synchronous try/catch to catch errors thrown later in a callback.

quiz.q: function f() { try { return "try"; } finally { console.log("cleanup"); } } — what does calling f() do?
options: Throws because return isn't allowed in try
quiz.explain: finally runs before the function actually returns, and here it doesn't override the return value.

concepts.name: Modules: import and export
concepts.summary: Split code into ES modules with named and default exports, static and dynamic imports.
concepts.why: Every modern JavaScript project — browser, Node.js or bundled — is organised as modules.
takeaways: Named exports are imported by name; a default export by any name
Imports are static, live and read-only; each module runs once
Use `import()` for lazy or conditional loading
pitfalls: Omitting the `.js` extension in browser or Node ESM relative imports.

quiz.q: Module a.js exports let n = 0 and a function inc() that increments it. b.js imports { n, inc } and calls inc(). What does b see in n?
quiz.explain: ES module imports are live views of the exporter's variables, so the update is visible.

concepts.name: Working with JSON
concepts.summary: Convert between JavaScript values and JSON text with JSON.stringify and JSON.parse, and know what gets lost.
concepts.why: JSON is the format of nearly every web API, config file and local storage entry.
concepts.body:
**JSON** is a text format based on JavaScript literals, but stricter: keys must be double-quoted strings, there are no comments or trailing commas, and the only values are strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, arrays and objects.

`JSON.stringify(value)` turns a value into JSON text; `JSON.parse(text)` turns text back into values. A third argument to `stringify` pretty-prints: `JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)`.

Not everything survives the round trip:

- `undefined`, functions and symbols are **dropped** from objects (and become `null` in arrays).
- `Date` objects become ISO strings (via their `toJSON` method) and come back as plain strings.
- `Map`, `Set` and class instances become plain `{}` or lose their prototype.
- `NaN` and `Infinity` become `null`.
- `BigInt` throws a `TypeError`.
- Circular references throw.

You can customise both directions. Objects can define `toJSON()` to control their serialised form. The second argument of `stringify` (a **replacer** function or array of keys) filters or transforms properties, and the second argument of `parse` (a **reviver**) transforms values on the way in — for example turning date strings back into `Date`s.

`JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` on invalid input, so wrap parsing of anything external — user input, files, `localStorage` — in `try...catch`.

A tempting trick, `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))`, makes a deep copy but silently loses dates, `undefined` and more. Use `structuredClone(obj)` instead.
takeaways: `stringify` drops undefined/functions, turns Dates into strings and Maps/Sets into {}
`JSON.parse` throws on bad input — guard external data
Use a reviver or `toJSON` to customise conversion; `structuredClone` for deep copies
pitfalls: Expecting dates to come back from `JSON.parse` as `Date` objects.

quiz.q: What does JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: 1 }) return?
quiz.explain: Properties whose value is undefined are omitted from JSON objects.

concepts.name: Map and Set
concepts.summary: Use Map for key–value lookups with any key type and Set for unique values, including the new set operations.
concepts.why: They are the right data structures for caches, lookups, de-duplication and membership tests.
concepts.body:
A **Map** stores key–value pairs where keys can be any value — objects, functions, numbers — not just strings:

```javascript
const visits = new Map();
visits.set(user, 3);
visits.get(user);   // 3
```

Its API: `set`, `get`, `has`, `delete`, `clear` and the `size` property. Maps remember **insertion order** and are directly iterable: `for (const [key, value] of map)`, plus `keys()`, `values()` and `entries()`.

Prefer a Map over a plain object when keys are dynamic or user-provided, when you add and remove a lot, or when keys aren't strings. Objects have inherited properties (`"toString" in {}` is true) and string-only keys; Maps have neither problem. Convert with `new Map(Object.entries(obj))` and `Object.fromEntries(map)`. `Map.groupBy(items, fn)` (ES2024) builds a Map of groups.

A **Set** holds unique values. `add`, `has`, `delete` and `size` work as you'd expect; `has` is fast compared to `array.includes` on large collections. The quickest de-duplication is `[...new Set(array)]`.

Both use **SameValueZero** equality: like `===`, except `NaN` equals `NaN`. Objects are compared by reference, so two different `{ id: 1 }` objects are two different keys.

ES2025 adds set algebra: `a.union(b)`, `a.intersection(b)`, `a.difference(b)`, `a.symmetricDifference(b)`, and `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom`. Each returns a new Set or a boolean.

`WeakMap` and `WeakSet` hold their object keys weakly, so entries vanish when the key object is garbage-collected — ideal for attaching metadata to objects you don't own.
takeaways: Map: any key type, insertion order, `size`, directly iterable
Set: unique values, fast `has`; `[...new Set(arr)]` de-duplicates
ES2025 sets have `union`, `intersection`, `difference` and friends
pitfalls: Using objects as Map keys and expecting a different-but-equal object to find the entry.

quiz.q: What is new Set([1, "1", 1, NaN, NaN]).size?
quiz.explain: 1 and "1" are different values, duplicates of 1 collapse, and SameValueZero treats NaN as equal to NaN: {1, "1", NaN}.

concepts.name: Event propagation and delegation
concepts.summary: Understand capture and bubbling, target vs currentTarget, and handle many elements with one listener.
concepts.why: Delegation keeps dynamic lists and tables fast and simple to wire up.
concepts.body:
When an event fires on an element, it travels through the DOM in three phases:

- **Capture**: from `window` down to the target's parent.
- **Target**: at the element where it happened.
- **Bubble**: back up from the target to `window`.

Listeners run in the bubble phase by default; pass `{ capture: true }` to run during capture instead. Most events bubble; some don't, notably `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter` and `mouseleave` (use `focusin`/`focusout` or `pointerover` when you need bubbling versions).

Inside a handler:

- `event.target` is the element where the event originated (maybe a deeply nested `<span>`).
- `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running.

`event.stopPropagation()` stops the event travelling further. Use it sparingly — it breaks other code (analytics, close-on-outside-click menus) that relies on bubbling. `preventDefault()` is unrelated: it cancels the default action but lets the event continue.

**Event delegation** uses bubbling to handle events for many elements with a single listener on a common ancestor. Combined with `element.closest(selector)`, which walks up from the target to the nearest matching ancestor, it looks like this:

```javascript
list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const button = e.target.closest("button[data-action]");
  if (!button || !list.contains(button)) return;
  ...
});
```

Benefits: one listener instead of hundreds, and elements added later work automatically with no extra wiring. Put the action and IDs in `data-*` attributes so the handler knows what to do.
takeaways: Events capture down, hit the target, then bubble up
`target` is where it started; `currentTarget` is where the listener is
Delegate with one ancestor listener + `closest()` for dynamic content
pitfalls: Calling `stopPropagation()` by habit, which silently breaks other listeners higher up.

quiz.q: A click on a <span> inside a <button> bubbles to a listener on the <ul>. What are event.target and event.currentTarget?
quiz.explain: target is where the event originated; currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently running.

concepts.name: Callbacks and timers
concepts.summary: Schedule work with setTimeout and setInterval and see why JavaScript code never blocks waiting.
concepts.why: Asynchronous callbacks are the foundation that promises and async/await are built on.
concepts.body:
JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, one piece at a time, and each piece **runs to completion** — nothing interrupts it. Slow operations (timers, network, disk, user input) don't block that thread. Instead you hand over a **callback** to be called later, and your code keeps going.

Timers are the simplest example:

- `setTimeout(fn, ms)` calls `fn` once, after *at least* `ms` milliseconds.
- `setInterval(fn, ms)` calls it repeatedly.
- Both return an ID; cancel with `clearTimeout(id)` / `clearInterval(id)`.

The delay is a minimum, not a guarantee: the callback runs only when the thread is free. Even `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs *after* the current code finishes. Browsers also clamp nested timers to at least 4 ms and throttle timers in background tabs.

Event handlers, `XMLHttpRequest` and older Node.js APIs all use callbacks. Node's convention is the **error-first callback**: `fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { ... })` — check `err` first.

Callbacks have real drawbacks once operations depend on each other:

- Nesting grows rightward into "callback hell".
- Each level must handle errors manually; a `throw` inside a callback can't be caught by a `try` around the code that scheduled it.
- It's easy to call a callback twice, or never.

Promises (next lesson) solve these by representing the future result as a value you can return, chain and combine. Timers themselves are still useful for delays, polling, and debouncing user input.
takeaways: Code runs to completion; callbacks run later when the thread is free
Timer delays are minimums; `setTimeout(fn, 0)` still waits for current code
Nested callbacks are hard to compose and to error-handle — promises fix that
pitfalls: Expecting `setTimeout(fn, 1000)` to fire exactly on time while heavy code is running.

quiz.q: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); console.log("C"); — what is the output order?
quiz.explain: The timeout callback can only run after the current script finishes, even with a 0 ms delay.

concepts.name: Promises
concepts.summary: Represent future results with promises: chain then/catch/finally and combine them with Promise.all and friends.
concepts.why: Every modern async API — fetch, file system, databases — returns promises.
concepts.body:
A **promise** is an object standing for a value that will be available later. It is in one of three states: **pending**, then either **fulfilled** with a value or **rejected** with a reason (usually an `Error`). Once settled, it never changes.

You react with methods that each return a *new* promise, which is what makes chaining work:

- `.then(onFulfilled)` — receives the value. Whatever you return becomes the next promise's value; if you return a promise, the chain waits for it.
- `.catch(onRejected)` — handles a rejection from *any* earlier step. Throwing inside a `then` rejects the chain too.
- `.finally(fn)` — runs either way, for cleanup.

```javascript
loadUser(id)
  .then(user => loadOrders(user.id))
  .then(orders => render(orders))
  .catch(showError);
```

Always return from `then` callbacks when you start more async work; forgetting `return` breaks the chain and the next step runs too early. Always end a chain with `catch` (or `await` it in a `try`): an unhandled rejection is reported as an error, and Node.js exits by default.

Combinators run promises concurrently:

- `Promise.all(ps)` — fulfils with an array of all values; rejects as soon as **any** rejects.
- `Promise.allSettled(ps)` — waits for all, giving `{ status, value | reason }` for each.
- `Promise.race(ps)` — settles like the first one to settle.
- `Promise.any(ps)` — the first to *fulfil*; rejects only if all reject.

To wrap a callback API, use the constructor: `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)`. `Promise.withResolvers()` (ES2024) returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` when you need to resolve from outside. `Promise.resolve(x)` and `Promise.reject(err)` create already-settled promises.
takeaways: A promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected — once
`then` returns a new promise; return values (or promises) to chain
`all` fails fast, `allSettled` waits for everything, `any` wants one success
pitfalls: Forgetting to `return` a promise inside `.then`, so the next step doesn't wait.
Leaving a chain without `.catch`, producing unhandled rejections.

quiz.q: You need results from three requests and want the others even if one fails. Which combinator fits?
quiz.explain: allSettled waits for every promise and reports each one's status, never rejecting early.

quiz.q: Inside .then(x => { fetchMore(x); }), fetchMore returns a promise. What does the next .then receive?
quiz.explain: The callback doesn't return anything, so the chain continues with undefined without waiting.

concepts.name: async and await
concepts.summary: Write asynchronous code that reads top to bottom with async functions, await and try/catch.
concepts.why: async/await is how almost all modern asynchronous JavaScript is written.
takeaways: An async function returns a promise; `await` unwraps one or throws
Start independent work together and `await Promise.all([...])`
`forEach` doesn't await — use `for...of` (sequential) or `Promise.all` + `map`
pitfalls: `items.forEach(async item => await save(item))` and assuming everything is saved afterwards.

quiz.q: getA() and getB() each take 1 s and are independent. How long does const a = await getA(); const b = await getB(); take?
options: It depends on which resolves first
quiz.explain: Each await waits before the next call starts, so the durations add up; Promise.all would take about 1 s.

quiz.q: What does an async function return when its body executes return 42?
quiz.explain: Async functions always return a promise; the returned value becomes its fulfillment value.

concepts.name: Making HTTP requests with fetch
concepts.summary: Request data from APIs with fetch, handle HTTP errors properly, send JSON and cancel requests.
concepts.why: Talking to servers is the core of most web apps, and fetch is the standard API in browsers and Node.js.
takeaways: fetch rejects only on network errors — always check `res.ok`
Reading the body (`res.json()`) is a separate await
Send JSON with method, Content-Type header and `JSON.stringify` body; cancel with AbortSignal
pitfalls: Assuming a 404 or 500 response makes fetch throw.

quiz.q: The server responds 404 Not Found. What does await fetch(url) do?
options: Resolves with a Response whose ok is false
quiz.explain: fetch only rejects on network-level failures; HTTP error statuses produce a normal Response with ok false.

concepts.name: Prototypes and inheritance
concepts.summary: See how property lookup walks the prototype chain and how classes, Object.create and built-ins fit on top of it.
concepts.why: Prototypes explain how classes, methods and instanceof actually work, and why some objects behave unexpectedly.
concepts.body:
Every object has an internal link, `[[Prototype]]`, to another object (or `null`). When you read a property that the object doesn't own, the engine looks it up on the prototype, then the prototype's prototype, and so on — the **prototype chain** — until it finds it or reaches `null` and returns `undefined`.

Writing is different: assigning `obj.x = 1` creates or updates an **own** property on `obj` (unless the chain has a setter), **shadowing** any inherited `x`.

Inspect and set the link with `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` and `Object.create(proto)`. You'll also see `obj.__proto__`; it's a legacy accessor — avoid it in new code. `Object.setPrototypeOf` exists but changing a live object's prototype is slow.

Classes are built on this. For `class Dog extends Animal`:

- methods are stored once on `Dog.prototype`, shared by every instance;
- each instance's `[[Prototype]]` is `Dog.prototype`;
- `Dog.prototype`'s `[[Prototype]]` is `Animal.prototype`, then `Object.prototype`, then `null`;
- static members live on the constructor, and `Dog`'s own prototype is `Animal`.

`instanceof` simply checks whether `Ctor.prototype` appears in the object's chain. Built-ins work the same way: `[].map` is found on `Array.prototype`.

Two practical consequences:

- `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` distinguishes own from inherited properties; `in` and `for...in` see inherited ones too.
- Plain `{}` inherits from `Object.prototype`, so `"constructor" in {}` is true. For a pure dictionary use `Object.create(null)` — or a `Map`.

Never add methods to built-in prototypes such as `Array.prototype` in application code; it collides with future standard methods and other libraries.
takeaways: Reads walk the prototype chain; writes create own properties
Class methods live on `Class.prototype`, shared by all instances
`instanceof` checks whether `Ctor.prototype` is in the chain
pitfalls: Extending built-in prototypes like `Array.prototype` in app code.

quiz.q: Where does the method area live for instances of class Square { area() {} }?
options: On each instance as an own property
quiz.explain: Methods declared in a class body are defined once on the class's prototype object and inherited by instances.

quiz.q: const p = { x: 1 }; const o = Object.create(p); o.x = 2; — what is p.x afterwards?
quiz.explain: Assignment creates an own property x on o that shadows p.x; the prototype is unchanged.

concepts.name: Iterators and generators
concepts.summary: Implement the iteration protocol, write generator functions with yield and chain lazy iterator helpers.
concepts.why: Iteration underlies for...of, spread and destructuring, and generators make lazy and infinite sequences easy.
concepts.body:
An object is **iterable** if it has a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an **iterator**: an object with a `next()` method that returns `{ value, done }`. Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, NodeLists and `arguments` are iterable, and everything that consumes iterables — `for...of`, spread, array destructuring, `Array.from`, `new Map(...)`, `Promise.all` — works with yours too.

Writing `next()` by hand is tedious. A **generator function** (`function*`) does it for you. Calling it returns a generator object without running the body; each `next()` resumes execution until the next `yield`, which produces a value and pauses:

```javascript
function* range(start, end, step = 1) {
  for (let i = start; i < end; i += step) yield i;
}
[...range(0, 10, 3)]   // [0, 3, 6, 9]
```

Generators keep their local state between calls, so they are naturally **lazy**: values are computed only when asked for. That makes infinite sequences possible, as long as the consumer stops. `yield* other` delegates to another iterable, handy for recursive structures like trees. A `return` inside ends iteration (`done: true`), and breaking out of `for...of` calls the generator's `return()` so its `finally` blocks run.

ES2025 adds **iterator helpers** on `Iterator.prototype`: `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `forEach` and `toArray`. Unlike array methods they are lazy and work on any iterator, including infinite ones. `Iterator.from(obj)` wraps any iterable or iterator so it gets these methods.

Make a class iterable by defining `*[Symbol.iterator]() { ... }` as a generator method.
takeaways: Iterable = has `[Symbol.iterator]()`; iterator = has `next()` returning `{ value, done }`
Generators pause at `yield` and are lazy — infinite sequences are fine
ES2025 iterator helpers (`map`, `filter`, `take`, `toArray`...) chain lazily
pitfalls: Spreading an infinite generator (`[...naturals()]`) — it never ends.

quiz.q: When does the body of a generator function start executing?
options: On the first call to next()
quiz.explain: Calling a generator function only creates the generator object; the body runs up to the first yield on the first next().

quiz.q: Why can naturals().map(f).take(3).toArray() finish even though naturals() is infinite?
options: Iterator helpers are lazy and take(3) stops pulling after three values
map converts it to an array of 1000 items first
toArray has a built-in length limit
quiz.explain: Each helper pulls one value at a time on demand, so take(3) simply stops requesting more.

concepts.name: Symbols and well-known symbols
concepts.summary: Create collision-free property keys with Symbol and customise language behaviour via well-known symbols.
concepts.why: Symbols are how the language exposes hooks like iteration and type conversion to your own objects.
concepts.body:
A **symbol** is a primitive whose only property is being unique. `Symbol("id")` creates a new one each time; the description is just a label for debugging, so `Symbol("id") !== Symbol("id")`.

Used as property keys, symbols can never clash with string keys or with symbols from other code:

```javascript
const meta = Symbol("meta");
obj[meta] = { cachedAt: Date.now() };
```

Symbol-keyed properties are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys`, `Object.entries` and `JSON.stringify`. They're not private — `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(obj)` and `Reflect.ownKeys(obj)` reveal them — but they stay out of the way of normal code. That makes them good for library metadata and for extending objects you don't own. For real privacy, use `#private` class fields.

`Symbol.for("app.key")` is the exception to uniqueness: it looks up a **global registry**, returning the same symbol for the same string everywhere in the agent, even across realms such as iframes. `Symbol.keyFor(sym)` gives the key back.

**Well-known symbols** are predefined symbols the language checks to let objects customise built-in behaviour:

- `Symbol.iterator` / `Symbol.asyncIterator` — make an object (async) iterable.
- `Symbol.toPrimitive` — control conversion to number or string (`+obj`, template literals).
- `Symbol.toStringTag` — the name shown by `Object.prototype.toString`, e.g. `[object Money]`.
- `Symbol.hasInstance` — customise `instanceof`.
- `Symbol.dispose` / `Symbol.asyncDispose` — used by the newer `using` declarations for automatic resource cleanup, already shipping in recent V8-based runtimes.

Implementing these protocols makes your objects feel native: they work with spread, template literals and `for...of` like built-ins do.
takeaways: Every `Symbol()` is unique; `Symbol.for()` shares symbols via a global registry
Symbol keys are hidden from keys/entries/JSON but not truly private
Well-known symbols (`iterator`, `toPrimitive`, `toStringTag`) hook into language behaviour
pitfalls: Treating symbol properties as private data — `Reflect.ownKeys` exposes them.

quiz.q: Which call lists a symbol-keyed property of obj?
quiz.explain: Reflect.ownKeys returns both string and symbol own keys; the others ignore symbols.

concepts.name: Proxy and Reflect
concepts.summary: Intercept fundamental object operations with Proxy traps and forward them correctly with Reflect.
concepts.why: Proxies power reactivity systems, validation layers, mocks and API wrappers.
concepts.body:
A **Proxy** wraps a target object and lets you intercept fundamental operations on it through **traps** defined in a handler:

```javascript
const p = new Proxy(target, {
  get(target, key, receiver) { ... },
  set(target, key, value, receiver) { ... },
});
```

There are traps for every internal operation: `get`, `set`, `has` (`in`), `deleteProperty`, `ownKeys` (`Object.keys`, `for...in`), `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `defineProperty`, `getPrototypeOf`, and for function targets `apply` (calls) and `construct` (`new`). Any trap you omit falls through to the target.

**Reflect** has a static method with the same name and signature for each trap. Use it to perform the default behaviour inside a trap: `return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)`. Passing `receiver` matters: it makes getters on the target (or its prototype chain) run with `this` set to the proxy, so accesses inside them are intercepted too. `Reflect.set` and friends also return booleans instead of throwing, which is exactly what traps must return.

Common uses:

- **Validation**: reject bad writes in `set`.
- **Reactivity**: record reads in `get`, trigger updates in `set` — Vue 3's reactivity is built this way.
- **Defaults / negative indexes / logging / mocks** for tests.

Limits and costs:

- The engine enforces **invariants**: e.g. a trap can't report a non-configurable property as missing; violations throw `TypeError`.
- A proxy is a different object: `proxy !== target`.
- Objects with internal slots break through proxies: `Map` methods and class `#private` fields fail when `this` is the proxy. Wrap the target's methods or avoid proxying such objects.
- Every operation goes through a function call, so proxies are slower than plain objects in hot paths.
takeaways: A Proxy intercepts operations via traps; missing traps forward to the target
Use `Reflect.*` inside traps, passing `receiver`, for correct default behaviour
Proxies break on internal slots (Map, #private) and cost performance
pitfalls: Returning nothing from a `set` trap: in strict mode a falsy result throws TypeError.

quiz.q: Why pass receiver to Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) in a get trap?
options: So getters run with this = the proxy, keeping nested accesses intercepted
quiz.explain: receiver becomes this for accessor properties, so getters see (and go through) the proxy instead of the raw target.

concepts.name: Regular expressions
concepts.summary: Match, extract and replace text with regular expressions, named groups and flags.
concepts.why: Validation, parsing logs and bulk text transformations all lean on regular expressions.
concepts.body:
A **regular expression** describes a text pattern. Write a literal `/pattern/flags`, or `new RegExp(string, flags)` when the pattern is built at runtime.

Core syntax: `\d` digit, `\w` word character, `\s` whitespace, `.` any character (except newlines unless the `s` flag), `[a-z]` sets, `^`/`$` anchors, `\b` word boundary, quantifiers `*`, `+`, `?`, `{2,4}` (add `?` for lazy: `+?`), alternation `a|b`, groups `( )`, non-capturing `(?: )`, **named groups** `(?<year>\d{4})`, and lookarounds `(?=...)`, `(?<!...)`.

Flags: `g` global, `i` case-insensitive, `m` multiline anchors, `s` dot matches newlines, `u` Unicode mode, `v` (ES2024) an upgraded Unicode mode with set operations, `y` sticky, `d` match indices.

The methods you'll use:

- `re.test(str)` — boolean.
- `str.match(re)` — without `g`, a match with groups (`m.groups.year`); with `g`, an array of all matched strings.
- `str.matchAll(re)` — iterator of full match objects for a `g` regex; the best way to extract many matches with groups.
- `str.replace(re, replacement)` / `replaceAll` — replacement strings can reference `$1` or `$<name>`, or pass a function.
- `str.split(re)`.

The classic trap: a regex with `g` or `y` is **stateful** — `test` and `exec` advance `re.lastIndex`, so reusing the same regex can alternate between `true` and `false`. Don't share global regexes for `test`.

When putting user input into a pattern, escape it. ES2025 adds `RegExp.escape(str)` for exactly that. And keep patterns modest: nested quantifiers like `(a+)+` can backtrack catastrophically on some inputs (ReDoS). For HTML, URLs and dates, prefer real parsers such as `URL` and `Intl`.
takeaways: Use named groups and `matchAll` to extract structured data
Regexes with `g`/`y` keep `lastIndex` state — don't reuse them for `test`
Escape user input (`RegExp.escape` in ES2025) and avoid nested quantifiers
pitfalls: Building a RegExp from user input without escaping special characters.

quiz.q: const re = /x/g; console.log(re.test("x"), re.test("x")); — what is printed?
quiz.explain: The first test sets lastIndex to 1, so the second search starts past the only x, fails and resets lastIndex to 0.

concepts.name: Immutability and copying
concepts.summary: Avoid accidental mutation with change-by-copy methods, structuredClone and Object.freeze — and know their limits.
concepts.why: Shared mutable state causes some of the hardest bugs, and UI frameworks rely on immutable updates.
concepts.body:
Objects and arrays are shared by reference, so a function that mutates its argument changes the caller's data. Many bugs — and every React state update — come down to whether something was mutated or replaced.

**Producing new values instead of mutating** is the main technique:

- Spread for shallow copies with changes: `{ ...user, name }`, `[...list, item]`.
- ES2023 **change-by-copy** array methods: `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with(index, value)` return new arrays, alongside `map`, `filter`, `slice` and `concat`.
- For nested updates, copy each level along the path you change and share the rest: `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, name } }`.

**Deep copies**: `structuredClone(value)` (browsers and Node 17+) copies nested objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, typed arrays, and even circular references. It throws a `DataCloneError` for functions and DOM nodes, and class instances come back as plain objects without their prototype.

**Freezing**: `Object.freeze(obj)` makes existing properties read-only and prevents adding or removing properties. Writes are silently ignored in sloppy mode and throw `TypeError` in strict mode (modules, classes). But freeze is **shallow**: nested objects remain mutable unless you freeze them too. `Object.seal` allows changing values but not adding or deleting keys; `Object.isFrozen` checks.

Remember `const` only prevents rebinding a variable; it doesn't freeze anything.

Trade-offs: copying costs allocation and time, which matters for large collections in hot loops. Libraries like Immer let you write mutating code that produces structurally shared immutable results.
takeaways: Prefer returning new values: spread, `toSorted`, `toSpliced`, `with`
`structuredClone` deep-copies (Maps, Dates, cycles) but not functions or prototypes
`Object.freeze` is shallow and only throws on writes in strict mode
pitfalls: Assuming `Object.freeze` protects nested objects.

quiz.q: What happens with structuredClone({ save() {} })?
quiz.explain: Functions can't be serialised by the structured clone algorithm, so it throws.

quiz.q: const a = [3, 1, 2]; const b = a.toSorted(); — what is a afterwards?
quiz.explain: toSorted returns a sorted copy and leaves the original array unchanged.

concepts.name: The event loop and microtasks
concepts.summary: Understand the call stack, task queue and microtask queue, and predict the order async code runs in.
concepts.why: Knowing the event loop explains UI freezes, ordering bugs and why await doesn't block.
concepts.body:
JavaScript runs on one thread per agent (window, worker or Node process). The engine executes code from a **call stack**; when the stack empties, the host's **event loop** decides what runs next.

There are two kinds of queued work:

- **Tasks** (macrotasks): running a script, timer callbacks, I/O callbacks, user events, `MessageChannel` messages. The loop takes **one** task at a time.
- **Microtasks**: promise reactions (`then`/`catch`/`finally` callbacks, and code after an `await`), `queueMicrotask(fn)` and `MutationObserver` callbacks.
